Neomys anomalus exhibits a highly elevated resting metabolic rate relative to its body size, a trait commonly observed in semi-aquatic soricine shrews that must offset substantial thermoregulatory costs. At a core body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], respirometry trials have measured a maximal basal oxygen consumption of 66.83 milliliters per hour [JOi = 66.83 milliliters per hour], a value that underscores the intense energetic demands of this species. This heightened metabolic throughput is supported by the shrew's relatively small adult size; individuals typically attain an ultimate wet weight of 15 grams [Wwi = 15 grams], a modest mass that facilitates heat dissipation during bouts of aquatic foraging. The thermal neutral zone for the species appears narrow, and maintaining the 35 °C [T = 35 °C] set point requires a constant supply of invertebrate prey. Comparative data suggest that this metabolic rate is among the highest recorded for any European soricid of similar mass, reflecting the ecological pressures of hunting cold-blooded prey in cool montane streams.

Weaning from the mother occurs at 29 days after birth [tx = 29 days after birth], maintained at the maternal thermal baseline of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], at which point the young are capable of endothermic regulation and begin to consume solid prey. This gradual transition from ectothermic dependence to independent thermogenesis is critical for survival, as the juveniles must achieve a stable thermal balance before they can exploit the cold aquatic environment of their riparian habitat.

This maturation schedule is typical of soricine shrews, which invest heavily in somatic growth to support a high-metabolism lifestyle before committing resources to gametogenesis. The juvenile period is thus a crucial life-stage bottleneck during which the shrew must develop the foraging proficiency needed to secure a constant supply of invertebrate prey. This abbreviated lifespan is a direct consequence of the species' extreme metabolic rate, which accelerates oxidative damage and cellular senescence relative to similarly sized terrestrial mammals. This life-history configuration — rapid development, early maturation, and short adult tenure — is emblematic of a species operating at the energetic frontier of mammalian thermoregulation.
